source.title: Out of Distribution, Out of Luck: Process Rewards Misguide Reasoning Models
source.authors: Alexey Dontsov; Anton Korznikov; Andrey V. Galichin; Elena Tutubalina

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some table formatting is flattened, and portions of long example generations are marked as skipped; neither affects the reported SAE feature result recorded here.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies process-reward-model performance and SAE features, not neuron poles, neuron explanations, or any of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The SAE feature analysis is adjacent to interpretability but concerns learned features in a reward model, not the claim's neuron poles or their jobs. The PRM benchmark results and linear-probe results likewise do not measure any listed version.
record.test_reason: The paper evaluates a process reward model on reasoning-model outputs and interprets SAE features in that PRM. It never audits individual neurons or neuron poles, never scores neuron explanations, and never builds neuron-based attribution graphs. Its only mention of superposition is a background citation in related work, so its results bear on none of V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. More precisely: the PRM improves standard math models but fails to improve, and sometimes degrades, reasoning-model performance (up to 14%). Linear probes show high reward predictability from early layers for reasoning outputs. 80% of the reasoning-preferential SAE features (40 of 50) detect formatting artifacts, so the authors conclude the PRM detects stylistic signatures rather than evaluating mathematical validity.
record.recipe_differences: Uses linear probes and SAEs to study a process reward model's handling of reasoning traces, rather than auditing neuron poles or testing neuron explanations.

fits_no_version.finding: Of 50 validated reasoning-preferential SAE features at layer 15 of Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B, 40 (80%) respond to formatting artifacts such as whitespace, Unicode and punctuation. The other 10 respond to mathematical content or discourse structure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features in a PRM that discriminate reasoning-model traces mostly track surface formatting rather than mathematical content.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 19th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 2: Short Papers
record.problems: The authors note that the analysis covers one PRM and three reasoning models; they lack the PRM's full training distribution, and interpretation of SAE features involves subjective manual inspection. The feature result concerns SAE features rather than individual neurons.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted PRM benchmark accuracy results and linear-probe reward-prediction results (Sections 3–4 and Table 2): they do not measure neuron interpretability or any listed claim version.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the relation from 'discusses' to 'cites_only' because the paper only cites superposition and SAE work as background. It does not argue about whether neurons are clean. I kept tranche T6.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-PRM
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed reasoning-preferential SAE features at layer 15 and categorized their activation patterns.
rows.measure: Share of validated reasoning-preferential SAE features interpreted as responding to superficial artifacts rather than mathematical content
rows.uncertainty: Validation across 36 held-out pairs; p < 0.001 after FDR correction; Cohen's d = 0.62
rows.note: The paper reports that the other 10 features showed mathematical content or discourse-structure detection. These are SAE features, not individual neurons or neuron poles.
rows.check: The measure is the share of 50 selected, reasoning-preferential SAE features (not neurons) that respond to formatting artifacts. It is a selected subset and not an interpretability share of all units, so it cannot speak to any version. The record's state 'observed' only describes the paper's own finding.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
